QC Workflow

A Practical LitBuy QC Workflow: What to Check Before You Ship

A repeatable framework for reading warehouse photos, checking variants and making a more disciplined ship-or-return decision.

Updated August 10, 2026 · 12 min read · Independent guide
GUIDE
2026
IN THIS GUIDE01 Why a checklist beats a quick glance02 Read the overview photos first03 Inspect details by product type04 Make a documented ship-or-return decision05 Use measurements without fooling yourself06 Separate lighting problems from product problems07 Design better additional-photo requests08 Handle common red flags proportionately09 Build a QC record that improves future orders10 A five-minute final review
Important

Service rules and shipping routes can change. Confirm current details inside LitBuy before paying.

A repeatable framework for reading warehouse photos, checking variants and making a more disciplined ship-or-return decision. This guide focuses on repeatable checks you can apply to the current listing and warehouse record rather than promises about any seller or batch.

01

Why a checklist beats a quick glance

Warehouse photographs are most useful when they answer a decision you defined in advance. If you open the image gallery without a checklist, your attention naturally goes to the most attractive overview shot. That can leave sizing, symmetry, hardware, edges or the selected color unexamined. A repeatable workflow turns the photographs from reassurance into evidence.

Start by reopening the exact seller listing and order variant. Record the selected size, color and model before looking at the warehouse set. Product links can change, so compare against the listing that corresponds to your order rather than a screenshot saved weeks earlier. The purpose is not to prove perfection. It is to identify visible mismatches while a return or exchange may still be possible.

  • Confirm the exact order variant
  • Compare overview shape before small details
  • Use measurements for fit-sensitive items
  • Decide within the current return window
02

Read the overview photos first

Begin with silhouette, proportions and color. Look at the item from the same distance across the full set. A shoe pair should appear balanced in length, toe shape and panel placement. A garment should sit flat enough to reveal sleeve length, hem alignment and obvious twisting. A bag should show the relationship between handles, body shape and hardware rather than only a close crop.

Color is difficult to judge under warehouse lighting. Compare all photos for consistency and look for a large deviation from the seller images, but avoid treating a small temperature shift as proof of the wrong shade. When color is critical, request a neutral-light photo or include a common reference object if the service allows it.

03

Inspect details by product type

Move from general form to the details that matter for the category. For footwear, check the pair together, the outsole, heel alignment, lacing area and visible glue marks. For garments, inspect front and back, cuffs, collar, print placement and the measurement reference. For bags, examine corners, edge paint, zipper tracks, handle attachment and the way metal parts align.

Do not spend equal time on every detail. A tiny cosmetic inconsistency that disappears in normal use may matter less than a wrong measurement, damaged zipper or visibly uneven pair. Rank findings as functional, fit-related or cosmetic. That ranking makes the final decision less emotional.

04

Make a documented ship-or-return decision

Finish with a short written decision: accept, request another photo, exchange, or return. Note the evidence that drove it. This prevents the common cycle of reopening the same photographs without learning anything new. If the images cannot answer a material question, ask for a targeted shot rather than another generic angle.

A spreadsheet can help you find a promising listing, but it cannot guarantee the seller's next batch. Treat each warehouse arrival as a new inspection. The strongest system combines curated discovery, a current listing check, category-specific QC and a clear deadline for action.

05

Use measurements without fooling yourself

A ruler in a photograph looks objective, but it still needs interpretation. First check where the measurement begins and ends. A garment chest width measured flat is not the same as full chest circumference; an outsole length is not automatically the same as usable internal shoe length. Compare the warehouse method with the seller's size chart before declaring a mismatch.

Allow for normal measuring variation. Soft fabric can stretch or bunch, and camera perspective can hide whether a ruler is truly parallel to an edge. A difference of a few millimeters may be measurement noise, while a several-centimeter gap on a fit-critical dimension deserves attention. Ask for a new measurement that names both endpoints when the original photo is ambiguous.

Build a personal tolerance before ordering. Decide which dimensions can vary and which cannot. Sleeve length may be flexible on an oversized hoodie, while waist width can determine whether trousers are wearable. This prevents you from applying the same rigid standard to every number and helps you request only evidence that can change your decision.

06

Separate lighting problems from product problems

Warehouse lighting often creates false alarms. Bright overhead lamps can flatten black fabric, exaggerate shine on synthetic materials or make cream appear yellow. Review the same area across multiple angles. If the color shift moves with the light, it is more likely a photographic effect; if a patch remains in the same physical location, it may be a stain or material inconsistency.

Reflections deserve the same caution. Metal hardware and glossy leather can mirror the warehouse ceiling, photographer or surrounding tables. Look for broken surface lines, dents and scratches that remain visible across views. A single bright streak is less informative than a mark with consistent shape in different photos.

When color accuracy is central to the purchase, request one neutral reference image rather than debating the existing set. Ask for the product beside plain white paper or under more neutral light if that option is available. The goal is not studio-grade color science; it is enough evidence to distinguish the ordered colorway from a materially different one.

07

Design better additional-photo requests

A useful request is narrow, located and testable. Replace “please check quality” with “photograph the left heel straight from behind” or “place the ruler across the chest from armpit seam to armpit seam.” Warehouse staff can act on those instructions, and the resulting image can answer a clear question.

Request scale when a defect may be small. A close-up without context can make a harmless thread look dramatic, while a distant overview can hide a damaged edge. Pair one contextual view with one close detail only when both are necessary. More photographs are not automatically more information.

Do not use additional photos to answer questions a photograph cannot reliably resolve. Images rarely prove fiber composition, long-term durability, waterproofing or electronic performance. For those claims, rely on the listing, seller communication, applicable inspection service and your willingness to accept uncertainty. Recognizing the boundary of QC photography is part of good QC.

08

Handle common red flags proportionately

Wrong size, wrong color, missing pieces, major damage and a clearly different model are high-priority findings because they affect function or order accuracy. Uneven pairs, broken fasteners and large stains belong in the same group. These issues justify prompt documentation and a return or exchange inquiry while the order remains eligible.

Cosmetic observations need context. Loose threads can often be trimmed; a small removable mark differs from permanent discoloration; minor packaging damage may not affect the item. Compare the flaw with the item's price, intended use and visibility at normal distance. Being disciplined does not mean rejecting everything—it means spending attention where it matters.

Also watch for inconsistency between the order record and the photographed item. The product can look attractive and still be the wrong variant. Check labels, included accessories and any seller-specific option codes. Order accuracy comes before evaluating whether the substitute is acceptable.

09

Build a QC record that improves future orders

Save a compact record for accepted and rejected items: seller, listing date, selected variant, warehouse date, key measurements, observed issue and final decision. Avoid claiming that one accepted item makes every future batch verified. The record is a dated observation, not a permanent seller rating.

Over several purchases, patterns become useful. You may learn that a particular seller's garment chart consistently runs small, that boxed products create avoidable parcel volume, or that certain details need a custom photo every time. Those lessons can improve the spreadsheet and your next order checklist.

A trustworthy directory should expose when a link was reviewed and provide a way to report a dead or misleading entry. That is more credible than a generic “verified” badge with no date or method. The long-term advantage comes from visible maintenance, careful language and a feedback loop between discovery and warehouse evidence.

010

A five-minute final review

When the evidence is complete, step away briefly and return for one final pass in the same order every time. Confirm the order variant, count the pieces, scan the overview views, review the category-specific details, check measurements and read any warehouse note. This catches omissions without restarting the entire inspection from zero.

Then ask one practical question: if this exact item arrived at home in the condition shown, would the identified issue change how you wear or use it? The question filters out anxiety created by extreme zoom while keeping functional defects visible. It also helps you compare a minor imperfection with the real cost and delay of an exchange.

Finally, record the decision and date. If you accept, move the item to parcel planning. If you need evidence, send one targeted request. If the order is wrong or materially defective, begin the return or exchange inquiry promptly. A short, consistent closing routine prevents both rushed acceptance and endless inspection.

Continue your research

Return to the spreadsheet, compare current listings and keep your decision notes tied to the exact item in your warehouse.

Shipping

How to Plan LitBuy Shipping Cost Before Building Your Haul

Understand chargeable weight, parcel dimensions and route restrictions before your warehouse becomes an expensive surprise.

Updated August 10, 2026 · 11 min read · Independent guide
GUIDE
2026
IN THIS GUIDE01 A shipping estimate is a planning range02 Understand chargeable weight03 Build compatible groups, not one giant haul04 Use a final pre-submission check05 Create a useful pre-order budget06 Model volumetric weight with real dimensions07 Compare routes on more than price08 Decide when splitting a parcel makes sense09 Treat rehearsal packing as information10 Keep a post-shipment cost record11 A practical parcel-planning worksheet
Important

Service rules and shipping routes can change. Confirm current details inside LitBuy before paying.

Understand chargeable weight, parcel dimensions and route restrictions before your warehouse becomes an expensive surprise. This guide focuses on repeatable checks you can apply to the current listing and warehouse record rather than promises about any seller or batch.

01

A shipping estimate is a planning range

International parcel pricing is not simply the sum of product weights. A route may charge the greater of actual and volumetric weight, add a base charge for the first weight unit, or restrict certain product types. That means the most useful early estimate is a range with clear assumptions, not a single number that looks precise.

LitBuy currently provides a public shipping estimator. Use it before ordering to compare destinations and broad parcel profiles, then estimate again after the warehouse has recorded item weights and dimensions. The packed parcel is the information that matters for the final payment.

  • Estimate before ordering
  • Recalculate after warehouse intake
  • Compare actual and volumetric weight
  • Check restrictions for every route
02

Understand chargeable weight

Actual weight is what the parcel weighs on a scale. Volumetric weight converts the space a parcel occupies into a billing weight. A light but bulky coat, shoe box or plush item may therefore cost more than expected. The divisor used for volumetric weight can vary by shipping line, so use the line's current rule rather than a generic formula copied from an old guide.

You can reduce wasted volume by removing unnecessary packaging when that is safe, folding soft goods efficiently and avoiding a parcel made mostly of empty space. Packaging changes also affect protection. Saving a small amount is not worthwhile if fragile items arrive damaged.

03

Build compatible groups, not one giant haul

Consolidation can reduce repeated base charges, but one parcel is not always the cheapest or safest answer. Batteries, liquids, food, branded goods and oversized products can face different route limits. A restricted item may remove otherwise suitable choices for the entire parcel.

Group items by route compatibility and physical profile. Dense clothing and accessories may work well together, while boxed footwear or fragile collectibles may need a different plan. Compare at least two scenarios: one consolidated parcel and two deliberate parcels. Include packaging and possible volumetric weight in both.

04

Use a final pre-submission check

Before paying, verify the destination, declared contents, parcel services, insurance choice, packed dimensions and the latest route notice. Confirm that any packaging-removal request is reflected in the rehearsal or parcel data. Keep room in the budget for a difference between an early estimate and the final charge.

Good shipping planning begins before the first purchase. When you understand how each item changes weight, volume and route eligibility, you can build a haul that remains sensible at checkout instead of trying to rescue the budget after everything reaches the warehouse.

05

Create a useful pre-order budget

Split the budget into product cost, domestic delivery to the warehouse, international shipping and a contingency amount. Many disappointing haul plans reserve nearly all available money for products and treat international delivery as an afterthought. Reverse that habit: choose a maximum delivered cost first, then work backward to the amount available for items.

Use three parcel scenarios rather than one. A low estimate assumes efficient packing and a suitable economical route. A working estimate uses realistic weights and dimensions. A high estimate allows for volumetric billing, limited route choice or a modest rate change. If the haul is only affordable in the optimistic scenario, it is not yet a stable plan.

Track cost per item only as a secondary measure. Dividing shipping evenly can make a bulky low-value item look harmless, even when that item is responsible for most of the added volume. Compare the parcel with and without each large object. The difference reveals its real shipping impact and helps you decide whether local purchase would be better.

06

Model volumetric weight with real dimensions

For early planning, measure or estimate the length, width and height of the packed item—not the product alone. Multiply those dimensions and apply the current divisor published for the route. Because routes can use different divisors and rounding units, calculate separately for each serious option. A formula remembered from another agent or last year may produce a false comparison.

Shoeboxes are a classic example. The shoes may be moderately heavy, but the box fixes a large rectangular volume around them. If collection value is not important, box removal can materially reduce chargeable weight. If the box protects the shape or matters to you, include it intentionally rather than being surprised later.

Soft goods can also become volumetric when packed loosely. Vacuum or compression services may reduce space for appropriate textiles, but compression can crease prints, damage structured garments or be unsuitable for some materials. Ask what the service changes, then balance volume savings against product risk.

07

Compare routes on more than price

The cheapest displayed route is not automatically the best value. Compare estimated delivery window, tracking quality, insurance terms, destination-country handoff, item eligibility and the way weight is rounded. A slightly higher quote can be rational when it offers clearer tracking or accepts the parcel without awkward repacking.

Read the current route notice immediately before submission. Seasonal congestion, destination disruptions and temporary restrictions can change the practical choice. Do not rely on an old community screenshot. It may describe a route name that now uses a different carrier, limit or price structure.

Think about customs processing as part of the route, not an afterthought. Follow the platform's current declaration process and the laws applicable to the destination. No spreadsheet can promise duty-free arrival or eliminate inspection risk. Avoid guides that present a declaration value as universally safe across countries and parcel types.

08

Decide when splitting a parcel makes sense

Split when item restrictions create incompatible route groups, when a very bulky object raises chargeable weight for everything, or when concentrating all value in one parcel creates unacceptable risk. A split can also help when one group is urgent and another can use a slower economical service.

Do the complete arithmetic. Two parcels mean two base charges, two packaging sets and potentially two customs events. A split that looks cheaper from per-kilogram rates alone may cost more after fixed charges. Compare final estimates for the actual packed groups rather than applying an average rate.

Avoid arbitrary weight targets borrowed from social posts. A five-kilogram parcel is not inherently optimal, and a larger parcel is not automatically dangerous. The sensible breakpoint depends on route pricing steps, dimensions, contents and your own risk tolerance. Let current route data determine the split.

09

Treat rehearsal packing as information

When a rehearsal or pre-packing option is available, its value is improved parcel data. You can see how packaging choices affect dimensions and chargeable weight before final submission. Use it when the parcel contains bulky boxes, structured goods or several items whose combined volume is difficult to predict.

Write packaging requests around outcomes. Specify which retail boxes may be removed, whether tags should remain, which fragile pieces need reinforcement and whether moisture protection matters. Vague instructions such as make it small can produce a parcel you did not intend. Clear priorities help the warehouse balance protection and size.

After rehearsal, compare the new packed data with the earlier planning range. If the number falls outside the range, identify why: extra protective material, an item not removed, a dimension that triggers volumetric weight or a route-specific rounding step. Understanding the difference is more useful than simply accepting or rejecting the quote.

010

Keep a post-shipment cost record

Record the route, packed weight, dimensions, paid amount, dispatch date, delivery date and any adjustment. Over time this creates a destination-specific reference that is more valuable than generic online averages. You will learn which product combinations produce efficient parcels and how accurate your early assumptions are.

Do not treat the record as a guaranteed future quote. Fuel surcharges, exchange rates, carrier policies and seasonal capacity change. Use historical parcels to improve the shape of your estimate, then refresh the price and restrictions for every new submission.

The goal is controlled uncertainty. You cannot know the exact delivered cost when the first product is still in a seller's warehouse, but you can avoid the largest surprises by planning a range, checking volume, grouping compatible items and verifying current route data at the decision points that matter.

011

A practical parcel-planning worksheet

Create one row per warehouse item with actual weight, estimated packed dimensions, category, restrictions, packaging preference and priority. Add a route-eligible column after checking the current estimator. This reveals conflicts early: a battery that removes an economical line, a shoe box that drives volume or a low-priority item that makes the parcel cross a pricing step.

Below the item rows, compare two or three parcel groups. For each group, calculate total actual weight, estimated volume, likely chargeable weight, fixed charge and contingency. Write assumptions beside the number. A quote without assumptions becomes misleading as soon as packaging or route eligibility changes; a range with notes remains useful.

Use the worksheet to make one decision at a time. Remove or regroup the item with the largest cost effect, recalculate, then compare the delivered value of keeping it. This is more reliable than repeatedly clicking random combinations in an estimator. When the warehouse provides final data, replace estimates with recorded numbers and preserve the difference for your next haul.

Continue your research

Beginner Guide

From Product Link to Warehouse: A Safer LitBuy Buying Process

A step-by-step beginner framework for checking a listing, ordering the right variant and reviewing the warehouse arrival.

Updated August 10, 2026 · 13 min read · Independent guide
GUIDE
2026
IN THIS GUIDE01 Treat every spreadsheet entry as a lead02 Order for evidence, not hope03 Use the warehouse as a decision point04 Plan the parcel only after inspection05 Read a product page like an order form06 Choose a first haul that is easy to learn from07 Understand order and warehouse statuses08 Use the return window deliberately09 Prepare a parcel without losing track of items10 Turn one completed haul into a better system11 The beginner checklist in one sequence
Important

Service rules and shipping routes can change. Confirm current details inside LitBuy before paying.

A step-by-step beginner framework for checking a listing, ordering the right variant and reviewing the warehouse arrival. This guide focuses on repeatable checks you can apply to the current listing and warehouse record rather than promises about any seller or batch.

01

Treat every spreadsheet entry as a lead

A spreadsheet saves discovery time, but it is not a permanent certificate of quality. Marketplace links change, sellers relist products and later batches can differ from earlier examples. Open the original listing and verify that the product, price, photos and variants still match the directory card before placing an order.

Read the listing for material claims, measurements, dispatch timing and seller notes. If a choice is represented only by a coded photo, match the code carefully. Save the selected variant and any important request in your order notes so that the warehouse arrival can be checked against a clear expectation.

  • Reopen the current seller listing
  • Check price and available variants
  • Save fit-critical measurements
  • Record the exact selected option
02

Order for evidence, not hope

Choose the size from measurements where possible instead of relying only on familiar labels. A medium from one seller can differ substantially from another. For shoes, check the measurement method and whether the listing uses internal length, insole length or a regional size conversion.

Keep order notes short and verifiable. Requests such as confirm the selected color or photograph the measurement are easier to act on than a vague request for best quality. If a key question cannot be answered by the listing, resolve it before ordering rather than expecting warehouse photography to reveal a hidden material specification.

03

Use the warehouse as a decision point

When the item status changes to stored, compare the intake information and photographs with your saved order details. Check quantity, color, size label, visible measurements and obvious damage. Review the current return window immediately. Waiting can remove the option to exchange even when the issue is clear.

If the standard photos do not show an important detail, ask for one targeted angle. A useful request names the exact feature and where it appears. Avoid ordering a large set of nearly identical photos, which adds noise without improving the decision.

04

Plan the parcel only after inspection

Accepted items should then be grouped by destination, route compatibility, weight and volume. Use LitBuy's current shipping estimator as a planning tool and confirm the packed parcel data before payment. Some products may be unsuitable for a preferred route, so check restrictions before combining everything.

The full process is simple but disciplined: discover, verify, order, inspect, plan and ship. Each stage answers a different question. Following the sequence is more reliable than trusting a spreadsheet card, a seller image or a single warehouse photograph on its own.

05

Read a product page like an order form

Separate marketing images from selectable options. The attractive photograph at the top may show a different color, accessory set or upgraded version from the default variant. Click every relevant option and confirm whether the thumbnail, price and description change. If the listing uses numbered or lettered choices, include that code in your saved note.

Check whether domestic delivery is included and whether the seller mentions delayed dispatch, made-to-order production or separate shipping. A very low item price can become less attractive after domestic freight or a long wait that leaves the rest of the haul sitting in storage.

Look for measurement methodology, not only a size table. Sellers may measure a garment flat, state body recommendations, or use manual measurements with a published tolerance. Those are different kinds of information. Save the one that can later be compared with a warehouse photo.

06

Choose a first haul that is easy to learn from

A beginner parcel should be manageable. Mixing fragile electronics, liquids, batteries, oversized décor and time-sensitive clothing creates too many route and inspection questions at once. Start with a small group of compatible, easy-to-measure items so you can understand the workflow without making one expensive parcel depend on every unfamiliar rule.

Limit the number of sellers and variants in the first round. This makes it easier to notice domestic delivery times, warehouse intake patterns and the quality of your own notes. The objective of the first haul is not maximum savings; it is to build a process you can repeat.

Set a total delivered budget and a stop point before ordering. Marketplace browsing encourages one more inexpensive item, but each addition changes parcel weight, volume and inspection workload. A planned shortlist is more useful than a crowded cart assembled because each individual price looked small.

07

Understand order and warehouse statuses

Agent dashboards divide the purchase into stages such as submitted, purchased, seller sent, warehouse received and stored. The exact labels can change, but the underlying sequence matters. A submitted order may still be waiting for purchase; a seller-sent order is not yet available for international shipping; a stored item is ready for your review.

Do not treat an estimated domestic delivery date as a guarantee. Sellers can delay dispatch, provide incomplete tracking or split an order. If one item stalls, decide whether it is important enough to hold the rest of the haul. Storage time should be considered when coordinating purchases from several sellers.

When a status looks inconsistent, open the order details and timeline before contacting support. Record the order number, current status and the specific event you expected. A precise question—tracking shows delivered two days ago but intake is not recorded—is easier to resolve than asking where is my order.

08

Use the return window deliberately

The return clock may depend on seller policy, marketplace rules and the stage of the agent order. Review the current deadline as soon as warehouse photos appear. Do not postpone inspection until every item arrives; an early product can lose its return option while you wait for a slow seller.

Before requesting a return, identify the reason and evidence. Wrong variant, missing part, damage and a measurement outside the stated tolerance are clearer than a general feeling that the item is not good enough. The seller may reject subjective claims, and domestic return freight or other costs may apply.

Compare the cost of the problem with the cost and delay of resolving it. A functionally wrong item should not be accepted merely to avoid a fee, but a minor fix may be more practical than an exchange that restarts domestic shipping. The right choice depends on usability, evidence and time—not on winning every dispute.

09

Prepare a parcel without losing track of items

Before selecting warehouse items, reconcile them with your order list. Confirm that every accepted piece is included once and every return or exchange is excluded. Similar product names and duplicate color variants make mistakes easy, so use order numbers or thumbnails rather than memory.

Group restricted or special-handling goods separately and compare eligible routes. Decide which retail packaging should remain. Keep protection for fragile or structured items, and remove unnecessary volume only where it does not undermine the product. Packaging is part of the shipping plan, not a universal yes-or-no choice.

At final submission, review the address, recipient format, parcel services, declared contents and paid amount. Save the parcel number and tracking reference. Once dispatched, follow the carrier events without reacting to every quiet day; international handoffs often create gaps between export and destination scans.

010

Turn one completed haul into a better system

After delivery, compare the result with your product and warehouse notes. Did the warehouse photos reveal the issues that mattered? Were your measurements useful? Which item created unexpected volume? A short post-delivery review converts the experience into better decisions instead of a collection of isolated impressions.

Update dead links and dated observations in your personal shortlist. If a seller's new batch differs, record the date rather than overwriting history with a permanent label. Share factual feedback: selected variant, order date, observable result and relevant measurements. That is more useful to other buyers than a one-word quality score.

A good beginner process becomes faster with repetition. You learn which evidence is worth requesting, which categories need measurements and which shipping assumptions are realistic for your destination. The spreadsheet then serves its proper role: a maintained discovery layer inside a broader, evidence-based buying workflow.

011

The beginner checklist in one sequence

Before ordering, confirm that the listing is current, the chosen variant is exact, the measurement method is understood and the delivered budget still works. Save only the information you will use later: product link, option code, size, color, seller notes and fit-critical dimensions. This record becomes the reference for warehouse inspection.

At warehouse intake, verify identity before quality. Check quantity, selected option and measurement, then examine overall shape and relevant details. Make a timely accept, photo, exchange or return decision. Do not wait for the rest of the haul when a return window may be running, and do not request photographs that cannot resolve the question.

For the parcel, reconcile accepted items, group them by route compatibility, compare actual and volumetric weight and confirm the latest service conditions. Save the parcel and tracking records after payment. Once delivered, review where your assumptions were right or wrong. That final review is what turns a first order into a repeatable, safer process.
